# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-16 (Extended v128)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Spring Year 4—Louis Philippe's reign, April 1832)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Faubourg Saint-Antoine; Faubourg Saint-Marceau; wine-shops (Seven Billiards on Rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques; Corinthe on Rue Mondétour; Café Musain); schools; English provincial towns (Dunstead, Staveford, Kelmere, Torton, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Kelford, Yarlby, Gulhaven, Wilwick, Wilholt, Quenford). **Environmental details**: Frost silvered hedges overnight; someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall; rain threatened; wind carries salt/tar scent; bees hum in lavender; children chase hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; smoke from chimneys lies flat; gulls quarrel over fish heads in harbor towns. Bells ring for vespers. Light goes early. River up in spring. Baker's boy often late; lines at oven grow long.

## Primary Locations
**GORBEAU HOUSE**: 50-52 Salpêtrière district. **JONDRETTE DEN**: Abject, fetid. Furniture: straw chair, infirm table, two pallets, straw beds. Walls: leprous, seamed, charcoal sketches, moisture. Fireplace with red-hot brazier. Dormer window (four broken panes). Colored engraving "THE DREAM" (Napoleon on blue column). **Wooden panel—Battle of Waterloo**: sergeant rescuer (Thénardier) carrying colonel victim (Pontmercy). Rope-ladder with hooks, verdigris candlestick.

**WINE-SHOPS (FAUBOURG SAINT-ANTOINE)**: Centers of revolutionary fermentation. Men openly discuss cartridge-making, plot readiness, armed resistance. Bourgeois visitors arrive in good coats, shake hands with "important" men, depart within ten minutes. Patriotic women embrace newcomers. Meetings periodic (8-10 persons) or open (room so full must stand). Mixed attendance: enthusiasm or merely passing to work. Wine-shop near point Saint-Eustache suspected as meeting place for principal leaders. Aug—, chief of Society aid for tailors, Rue Mondétour, serves as intermediary between leaders and Faubourg Saint-Antoine.

**FAUBOURG SAINT-ANTOINE CHARACTERISTICS**: Peopled like ant-hill, laborious, courageous, angry as hive of bees. Quivering with expectation, desire for tumult. Lively yet sombre physiognomy. Poignant distress hidden under attic roofs; rare and ardent minds. Dangerous when distress and intelligence meet at extremes. Receives counter-shock of commercial crises, failures, strikes, slack seasons. Population full of proud virtue, capable latent heat, always ready to fly to arms. Powder-house of suffering and ideas at very gates of Paris. Wine-shops function as prophetic spaces where hearts swell, souls enlarge. Like taverns of Mont Aventine on cave of Sibyl, communicating with profound sacred breath. Reservoir of people; revolutionary agitations create fissures through which trickles popular sovereignty. Even when led astray, remains great (_Ingens_).

## Crisis at Gorbeau House: Resolution
**M. Leblanc's binding and struggle**: Remained impassive despite brutal assault. Overturned furniture, moved toward window. Despite binding, preserved silence, forgot anxiety for own life.

**Thénardier's metamorphosis**: Transformed from ferocious robber into polished negotiator. Devised scheme: wife to dress as before, hunt up "the Lark" (Cosette) with letter from M. Leblanc. Girl will follow into carriage; outside barrier, trap with two horses waits. Young lady will be taken by comrade in other vehicle; wife returns to report. **Threat**: "If you have me arrested, my comrade will give a turn of his thumb to the Lark."

**M. Leblanc's extraordinary escape (turning point)**: Concealed coin piece when searched; unscrewed and used as saw to cut cords. Before seven men could act, stretched hand to brazier. **Brandished above his head the red-hot chisel, emitting threatening glow**. All huddled in amazement. While red-hot iron sank into smoking wound, **impassive and almost august, he fixed on Thénardier his beautiful glance, in which there was no hatred, and where suffering vanished in serene majesty.**

**Javert's ambush and final escape**: Javert (tall man, square face, thin firm mouth, thick gray whiskers) positioned outside with men. Grew impatient, took action before Marius's signal. Ruffians terrified, seized abandoned arms (meat-axe, key, bludgeon, shears, pincers, hammers). Thénardier had knife. **Thénardier woman snatched enormous paving-stone, hurled at Javert's head; Javert ducked; stone struck wall behind.** **M. Leblanc's escape**: Took advantage of confusion, darkness, diverted attention. Dashed out window (door guarded, window not).

## Marius Pontmercy: Crisis of Conscience (Unresolved)
**Identity and age**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. **Paternal legacy**: Colonel's written instruction regarding Waterloo sergeant Thénardier. Recognized Thénardier in Waterloo painting.

**Unprecedented perplexity**: For last hour, two voices in conscience—one enjoining respect for father's testament, other crying to rescue prisoner. Extraordinary moral dilemma: everything depended on Marius. If he fired pistol, M. Leblanc saved, Thénardier lost; if not, M. Leblanc sacrificed. Father once saved by Thénardier at Waterloo. Yet M. Leblanc now victim of Thénardier's ambush. Moral obligation to both. **Crisis outcome unclear.**

## Girl (Cosette) and M. Leblanc Identity
**Girl identity clarified**: Handkerchief bore letters U. F., meaning Urbain Fabre. M. Leblanc is Monsieur Fabre—girl's biological father. Cosette became convent scholar; believes Valjean is her father. Marius recognizes: the "girl" he worshipped is Cosette, Thénardier's captive held for ransom scheme.

## Jean Valjean
Valjean integrated as convent assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete. Fauchelevent sole ally aware of full presence.

## English Provincial Towns: Population Movements and Daily Life (Fact vs. Mundane)
**Population movements (documented)**: Peten Haskick moved to Quenford; Lura Haskick followed. Kadrek moved to Wilholt. Zalis Corrley's daughter settled Wilholt. Kadan Corrley took Yewyn Corrford in marriage at Kelmere. Quiet Jotho married eldest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth at Ostcombe; couple lived there. **That spring, coughing sickness took Nelan; buried at Kelford.** Families involved: Stenworth, Prydenridge, Thornmere, Lindmere, Brackick.

**Daily mundane activities (recorded observations)**: Sorting old letters, mending torn sleeves, scrubbing steps, humming childhood tunes. Fewyn Stenworth and Rorald argued with carter over oats price. Thizek argued with carter over sack of oats. Pelia Lindmere and Havie Prydenridge read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Luena Stenenridge read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Nerine mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Volan watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly. Volia hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Luena Stenenridge gave jade mirror to Rozek. Rozek complained of aching back. Luena laughed at story nobody else found funny. Kassa Brackick counted coins twice, came up penny short. Marald counted coins twice, still came up penny short. Jotho counted coins twice, still came up penny short. Ulrald Corrford remarked: "The price of salt is a scandal"; Fenelle agreed. Gadrek Prydenridge laughed at story nobody else found funny. Wenelle talked for weeks of going to Ravenmere, yet stayed where was. Wenelle Lindmere remarked: "The price of salt is a scandal"; Gadrek agreed. Movie bought ribbon at stall, regretted it. Yera mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Isvie watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly. In Ostcombe, Luvie Prydenridge walked long way round to avoid muddy square. Jotho Thornmere remarked: "I heard the river is up again"; Luvie said it always was in spring. Dog barked at nothing, then went quiet. Weather, harvest, river conditions constant conversation topics. **Note**: Ulrald was apprenticed anew and became a smith.

## Historical Context: The Restoration, Revolution of July, and Current Fermentation (1815-1832)
**Bourbon Restoration critique**: House of Bourbon returned after Napoleon fell. Believed it bestowed rights and could take back charter rights. Did not understand roots of French society not fixed in Bourbons but in nations.

**Restoration's fatal decision (1830)**: Contested collective title and individual right of nation to sovereignty, citizen to liberty. Denied to nation that which made it a nation.

**Fifteen years of intellectual progress (1815-1830)**: Great principles—equality before law, liberty of conscience, speech, press—worked in perfect peace. Bourbons were instrument of civilization which broke in Providence's hands.

**Revolution of July (1830)**: Hardly produced shock; did not treat vanquished royalty as enemy. Mysterious respect springs from events where we sense collaboration of someone working above man.

**Louis Philippe (Winter/Spring Year 4)**: Handsome in old age, remained graceful; not always approved by nation, always by masses. Lacked majesty; wore no crown, no white hair. Mixture of noble and bourgeois suited 1830. Incorruptible; went out with umbrella. Policy domestic rather than national; excessive timidity displeasing to people. Deep tenderness toward family. One daughter, Marie d'Orleans, placed race among artists. Press free, tribune free, conscience and speech free. **What can be said: Louis Philippe, from point of view of human goodness, will remain one of best princes who ever sat on throne.**

**Cloud gathering (Spring Year 4)**: Strange shade gradually drew nearer, extended over men, things, ideas—shade from wraths and systems. Everything hastily stifled, moving, fermenting. Piles of shadows covered horizon. Electric tension such that first comer, stranger, brought light. Deep and dull mutterings allowed judgment of quantity of thunder contained by cloud. **Ever since 1830, petty partial revolts suppressed but ever bursting forth afresh—sign of vast underlying conflagration.**

## Revolutionary Fermentation and Secret Societies (Spring 1832)
**Public agitation and cartridge-making**: Workmen openly proclaim cartridge-making. "In less than a fortnight we shall be parallel with the government. With twenty-five thousand men we can face them." "I don't sleep at night, because I make cartridges all night." Soldiers' arms coveted. Remarks in low tone: "The plot is ripe, the matter is arranged." Woman sweeping doorsteps remarks: "For a long time, there has been a strong force busy making cartridges." Bourgeois talk peaceably to working-classes: "How is the rising coming along?" in tone of "How is your wife?" Police raids: April 5, agents arrested Pardon at five o'clock in morning while preparing cartridges (later killed in Barricade-Merry section, April 1834 insurrection). Weapons transfer: Two men met between Barrière Picpus and Barrière Charenton, near wine-shop with "Jeu de Siam"; one handed pistol to other; powder damp from chest perspiration; pistol reprimed with additional powder.

**Proclamations and public documents**: Proclamations addressed to National Guard in departments signed by _Burtot, wine-merchant_. **"Our doctrines are trammelled, our proclamations torn, our bill-stickers spied upon and thrown into prison."** **"The future of nations is being worked out in our obscure ranks."** **"Action or reaction, revolution or counter-revolution."** **"On the day when we cease to suit you, break us, but up to that day, help us to march on."**

**Suspicious activities (April 4, 1832)**: Passer-by mounted post at corner of Rue Sainte-Marguerite, shouted: "I am a Babouvist!" Beneath Babeuf, people scented Gisquet. At nightfall, workman warned by "very well dressed man" near canal: "Don't be alarmed, I am an agent of the committee. You are suspected. If you reveal anything, there is an eye fixed on you."

**Discovered documents**: Mason left package on bench near bridge of Austerlitz: two printed dialogues signed _Lahautière_, song "Workmen, band together," tin box full cartridges. In ditch between Père-Lachaise and Barrière du Trône, children discovered: bag with bullet-mould, wooden punch for cartridge preparation, wooden bowl with hunting-powder grains, cast-iron pot with melted lead traces.

**The cipher document (April 15, 1832)**: Carpenter picked up torn papers; one extremely significant. Document bore: Q, C, D, E with instruction: "Learn this list by heart." **Letters meant: quinturions, centurions, decurions, éclaireurs [scouts]; date u og a' fe = April 15, 1832.** Under each capital letter: names with characteristic notes and armaments. Q. _Bannerel_ (8 guns, 83 cartridges, safe man). C. _Boubière_ (1 pistol, 40 cartridges). D. _Rollet_ (1 foil, 1 pistol, 1 pound powder). E. _Tessier_ (1 sword, 1 cartridge-box, exact). _Terreur_ (8 guns, brave).

**Unité document**: Lists names and locations—Blanchard: Arbre-Sec. Complete nomenclature of sections of fourth arrondissement of Society of Rights of Man, with names and dwellings of section chiefs. Foundation of Society appears posterior to document date; possibly rough draft.

**Secret society network and structure**: From associations of Friends of the People (public and secret) sprang Society of the Rights of Man (dated one of orders of day: _Pluviôse, Year 40 of republican era_; survived Court of Assizes dissolution order). Society of the Rights of Man engendered Society of Action (impatient individuals who broke away). Other associations: Gallic Society; committee of organization of Municipalities; associations for liberty of press, individual liberty, instruction of people against indirect taxes. Society of Equal Workingmen (divided into three fractions: levellers, communists, reformers). Army of the Bastilles (cohort organized on military footing: four men commanded by corporal, ten by sergeant, twenty by sub-lieutenant, forty by lieutenant; never more than five men knew each other; creation combining precaution with audacity, stamped with genius of Venice). Société des Amis de l'A B C affiliated to Mutualists of Angers and Cougourde of Aix; met at Café Musain. Young men assembled at restaurant wine-shop Corinthe on Rue Mondétour. Meetings both secret and public. Manuel section reported; interrogatory revealed instructions from central committee.

**Military infiltration and recruitment**: Army mined at same time as population (proved by operations of Béford, Luneville, Épinard). Counted on: fifty-second regiment, fifth, eighth, thirty-seventh, twentieth light cavalry. In Burgundy and southern towns, planted liberty tree (pole surmounted by red cap). Schools as moved as faubourgs. Café Rue Saint-Hyacinthe and wine-shop Seven Billiards, Rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques, served as student rallying points.

**Revolutionary fermentation characteristics**: Fermentation public, one might almost say tranquil. Approaching insurrection preparing storm calmly before government. Artery beating everywhere. Network of secret societies spreading over country like membranes arising from certain inflammations. Not a point in Paris nor France exempt from it.
